MSK–SKIN · WEEK 13 · LECTURE 06 · LECTURE COMPANION

Peripheral Nervous System:
Somatic and Autonomic

Dr. Mindy Johnson · Anatomy of autonomic motor routes and visceral sensory pathways

Somatic vs ANSSympathetic RoutesParasympathetic & ENSVisceral & Referred PainMaster TheseFirst Aid

Learning objectives

  1. Define the ANS and distinguish it from somatic motor control.
  2. Compare sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric pathways by organization and function.
  3. Trace autonomic routes to their targets.
  4. Explain visceral afferent routes and referred pain.

Study order: learn the common sympathetic entry pathway first; then repeatedly trace each of the four sympathetic options before moving to the parasympathetic and visceral sensory pathways.

LEARNING OBJECTIVE 1

Somatic versus autonomic: trace the entire signal route

The first split is direction, not organ. Afferent sensory fibers travel toward the CNS; efferent motor fibers travel away from the CNS. Somatic pertains to the body wall and limbs; visceral pertains to organs. Somatic and visceral sensory pathways both exist, but the autonomic nervous system (ANS) describes the visceral efferent control pathways emphasized here.

FeatureSomatic motor (efferent)Visceral motor (ANS)
TargetSkeletal muscleSmooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands
Neuron chainOne motor neuron from CNS to muscleTwo neurons: preganglionic → autonomic ganglion → postganglionic
Motor soma originSomatic motor neurons at spinal cord levels and selected cranial motor nucleiSpecific brainstem nuclei and sympathetic/parasympathetic spinal cord segments
Peripheral ganglionic synapseNone along motor pathCharacteristic synapse in autonomic ganglion

Where does the autonomic synapse occur?

Paravertebral ganglia make the sympathetic chain along either side of the vertebral column. Prevertebral ganglia cluster along the abdominal aorta, often adjacent to major unpaired branches. Intrinsic/terminal (intramural) ganglia lie in or near the target organ. Location helps predict the pathway.

Retrieval checkpoint 1: A visceral motor axon leaves the CNS and ends in a ganglion. What neuron connects that ganglion to its target? Why is this not the usual somatic skeletal-muscle pattern?
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 2–3

Sympathetic outflow: the common entry route and four possible courses

Origin: the thoracolumbar sympathetic division has preganglionic cell bodies in the intermediolateral cell column (IMLCC), approximately T1–L2/3 in the professor's slides. Preganglionic fibers enter the sympathetic chain before diverging along one of four routes. Their broad function is the “fight-or-flight” response.

The on-ramp and off-ramp

White ramus communicans carries preganglionic sympathetic axons into the sympathetic trunk and is found at T1–L2/3. Gray ramus communicans carries postganglionic sympathetic fibers back to spinal nerves and occurs at all spinal levels. Both connect to the ventral ramus, not directly to a dorsal root.

Learn the shared starting sequence exactly

IMLCC (T1–L2/3) → ventral rootlets/ventral root → mixed spinal nerve → ventral ramus → white ramus communicans → sympathetic trunk. From there, four courses are possible:

CourseWhat preganglionic fibers doPostganglionic route / targets
1. AscendAscend in trunk and synapse at a superior ganglionHead via superior cervical ganglion and periarterial route; neck/upper limb via gray rami; cervical cardiopulmonary splanchnics
2. Same levelSynapse at entry levelMiddle trunk via gray ramus; thoracic cardiopulmonary splanchnics
3. DescendDescend below entry level and synapseLower trunk and lower limb via gray rami and spinal nerve rami
4. Pass throughNo synapse in trunk; travel as abdominopelvic splanchnic nervesSynapse in prevertebral ganglia; postganglionic fibers follow arterial branches to abdominopelvic viscera

The slide names celiac, superior mesenteric, aorticorenal, and inferior mesenteric ganglia as prevertebral locations. Don't confuse them with the paravertebral chain.

Retrieval checkpoint 2: Trace the sympathetic route from T1 to a sweat gland in the hand. At what point are gray and white rami used?
Retrieval checkpoint 3: A preganglionic fiber passes straight through the sympathetic chain. Where does it synapse, and what structure guides the postganglionic axon?
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 2–3

Parasympathetic and enteric divisions: distinguish outflow, ganglia and function

Parasympathetic = craniosacral outflow. Preganglionic neurons arise from brainstem nuclei associated with CN III, VII, IX, X and the S2–S4 sacral region. Its broad function is “rest and digest.” Unlike the thoracolumbar sympathetic chain model, parasympathetic ganglia are commonly near or within their targets.

Trace the parasympathetic pathways

OriginPreganglionic routeWhere fibers synapse
CN III, VII, IXCranial nerve outflow to head and neckNamed head parasympathetic ganglia: Ciliary, Otic, Pterygopalatine, Submandibular — COPS
CN X (vagus)From brainstem to thoracic and abdominal visceral targetsCardiac, thoracic and enteric/intrinsic ganglia associated with target organs
S2–S4Pelvic splanchnic nerves → pelvic plexusesIntrinsic ganglia near or in pelvic target organs

Enteric nervous system: two specific plexuses

The enteric nervous system can coordinate local digestive functions without requiring a new instruction from the CNS for every movement or secretion, although sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers modulate it. The lecture calls it the “gut brain” and identifies around 200 million neurons.

PlexusWhere to find itPrimary function
Myenteric (Auerbach)Between circular and longitudinal layers of muscularis externaGI smooth-muscle motor control and peristalsis
Submucosal (Meissner)Submucosa, especially intestinesGlandular secretion, electrolyte/water handling, local blood flow
Retrieval checkpoint 4: Which cranial nerves convey parasympathetic outflow, and how does the route from S2–S4 differ from a thoracic sympathetic route?
Retrieval checkpoint 5: Which enteric plexus controls peristalsis and which mainly modulates secretion and local blood flow?
LEARNING OBJECTIVE 4

Visceral afferents, pelvic pain line and referred pain

Visceral afferent fibers carry sensation from organs, glands and blood vessels toward the CNS. Information may be reflexive or nociceptive (pain-related). Visceral pain is commonly dull and poorly localized, in contrast to the relatively precise localization of many somatic cutaneous stimuli.

The pelvic pain line predicts a return route

Per the professor's simplified teaching model, visceral pain arising above the pelvic pain line generally travels back alongside sympathetic pathways to dorsal root ganglia around T1–L2. Pain arising below the line in the pelvic cavity generally follows parasympathetic pathways to S2–S4. The line approximates the inferior limit of parietal peritoneum. Treat this as a clinical routing rule, not a claim that every visceral afferent follows the same path.

Referred pain: why the painful site is misleading

Referred pain occurs when visceral and somatic afferents converge onto shared central pathways. Higher brain centers may interpret the signal as coming from a somatic region of the same segmental distribution rather than the organ. The lecture's supplemental example is angina pectoris, with cardiac pain perceived in the chest, left upper limb, back, neck or jaw.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT: Sudden pain in the chest or arm should never be dismissed as “only referred pain.” The mechanism explains location, but diagnosis requires clinical evaluation.
Retrieval checkpoint 6: A pelvic organ is below the pelvic pain line. Which autonomic route tends to accompany its pain afferents, and which spinal levels receive them?
Retrieval checkpoint 7: Why can myocardial ischemia produce discomfort in the left arm even though the arm itself is not ischemic?

MASTER THESE BEFORE MOVING ON

  1. Somatic motor is a one-neuron path to skeletal muscle; autonomic visceral motor normally uses pre- and postganglionic neurons.
  2. White rami bring preganglionic sympathetic axons into the trunk only at T1–L2/3; gray rami return postganglionic axons at all levels.
  3. Know the four possible sympathetic trunk courses and especially the unsynapsed abdominopelvic splanchnic route.
  4. Parasympathetic origin = CN III, VII, IX, X plus S2–S4; COPS and pelvic splanchnics are different pathways.
  5. Auerbach drives motility; Meissner drives secretory/vascular functions; visceral referred pain depends on afferent convergence.

THE MOST USEFUL FIRST AID CONNECTIONS

FIRST AID CONNECTION: Preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine at nicotinic ganglionic receptors; most sympathetic postganglionic targets receive norepinephrine, with sweat glands a prominent acetylcholine exception. This neurotransmitter layer is supplemental to the anatomical pathways emphasized by these lecture slides.
FIRST AID CONNECTION: Horner syndrome can follow interruption of a sympathetic pathway to the head (classically ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Use it as a route-localization example, not an additional lecture disease.
FIRST AID CONNECTION: Autonomic dysreflexia after certain spinal cord injuries and orthostatic hypotension from autonomic dysfunction both illustrate the clinical importance of intact efferent routes; these syndromes are not directly covered by the professor's slide deck.

Scope: The primary teaching throughout remains Dr. Johnson's 33-slide lecture, especially her spinal-level diagrams and pathways.
